title: Reading news impact
summary: How to tell whether a kind of news really moves a market: line events up, compare with random days, count days not headlines, and correct for trying many topics.

lessons.title: One headline is an anecdote
body: After a big headline, a market moves, and it is tempting to say the news caused it. But markets move every day. One example cannot tell you whether that kind of news usually matters.
The picture lines up the days around one news day, then a handful of them. Each path is noisy. Some go up after the news, some go down.
To learn anything, you need many events of the same kind, lined up the same way.

visual.alt: Price paths around a news day, from 10 days before to 10 days after. First one path, then five, each noisy and going different ways.

steps.caption: What a market did around one news day.
Five news days of the same kind. They do not agree.

inParity.label: The biggest market days and what was in the news

check.q: A market rose after one OPEC headline. What does that show?
options: Very little: one example cannot separate news from everyday noise
The market will rise next time
check.why: Markets move every day. One event is an anecdote.

check.q: What do you need to study a kind of news?
options: Many events of the same kind, lined up the same way
check.why: Many events let the noise average out.

lessons.title: Line events up on day zero
body: An **event study** lines up many events so the news day is day zero, then averages what happened before and after. Noise in each path tends to cancel; a real effect tends to remain.
Parity measures each move against the asset's normal daily move over the year before, so a calm asset and a wild one can be compared.
The average is only as good as the number of events behind it. Parity shows that number next to every result.

visual.alt: Forty faint price paths around a news day, with their green average line rising a little after day zero.

steps.caption: Forty events of the same kind, lined up on the news day.
Their average, in green. Noise mostly cancels; a drift after the news remains.

options: Noise tends to cancel while a real effect remains
check.why: Averaging reduces random noise in proportion to the number of events.

check.q: Why does Parity scale moves by each asset's normal daily move?
options: So calm and wild assets can be compared
check.why: A 1% move means more for a calm asset than for a wild one.

lessons.title: Compare with random days
body: An average after the news is not enough. Markets drift, and big days cluster. The fair question is: did news days do better than ordinary days?
Parity compares every event study with random days from the same years. The p-value comes from those random days, so fat tails and drift are already in the baseline.
The grey band shows where the average of the same number of random days usually lands. If the news line stays inside it, the pattern could be luck.

visual.alt: The green average of forty news days rises after day zero and leaves a grey band that shows where averages of random days usually land.

steps.caption: The average after forty news days.
The grey band: where an average of forty random days usually lands.

check.q: Why compare news days with random days?
options: Markets drift and have fat tails, so ordinary days are the fair baseline
check.why: The question is whether news days differ from ordinary ones.

check.q: The news average stays inside the random-day band. What does that suggest?
check.why: Random days often do just as well.

lessons.title: Count days, not headlines
body: Ten headlines about the same meeting are one event, not ten. Parity counts days, not items, so one busy news day does not look like a lot of evidence.
Events close together share the same market moves. Parity marks events within 20 trading days of another and repeats the averages using only the ones that do not overlap.
Under 5 events there is no p-value at all. Under 20 there is a warning.

visual.alt: Made-up example: 120 headlines collapse to 45 event days, and to 28 events that do not overlap.

steps.caption: Made-up example: 120 headlines on one topic.
Headlines on the same day count once: 45 event days.
Keep only events at least 20 trading days apart: 28.

check.q: Five headlines about the same rate decision on one day count as:
Below how many events does Parity give no p-value?
check.why: Under 5 there is no p-value; under 20 there is a warning.

lessons.title: Many topics, many false hits
body: Parity precomputes studies for 21 topics and 13 assets: 273 pairs. Even if no news mattered at all, some pairs would look strong by chance.
The picture shows that: scores for 273 pairs with no real effect, and the best one still looks impressive. It is the same trap as testing many strategies.
So rankings report a q-value, the p-value corrected for how many pairs were tried, and are sorted by it, never by the size of the move. Every result describes the past. None is a prediction.

visual.alt: A histogram of pattern strength for 273 topic and asset pairs with no real effect. The best one, marked in yellow, still reaches near 3; a red line shows about where luck alone reaches.

params.note: Every bar counts topic and asset pairs with no real effect

steps.caption: One topic and asset pair with no real effect.
All 273 pairs. The best looks strong by chance.
The red line: about where luck alone reaches with that many pairs.

inParity.label: News impact search, ranked by q-value

check.q: Why can't you rank topics by the biggest average move?
options: It rewards topics with few events and lucky outliers
check.why: Thin topics with one dramatic event would top the list.

check.q: What does a q-value correct for?
check.why: It is the p-value adjusted for the number of tests.
